title: ME05b: Simple Rules for the System
author: Richard Claydon
summary: This second part completes Claydon's five simple rules through the fictional leader Maya, moving from role to system. Rule three is to calibrate for the level a person is in while coaching for the next, using a reworked version of Jaques's levels of work to diagnose who is overstretched, stuck, hesitant or coasting. Rule four is to anchor what matters through six recurring questions that become team habits. Rule five is to read the system rather than ride it, using five lenses of purpose, structure, enterprise, narrative and emergence. The thread is that leaders cope with complexity through repeatable practices and attention, not heroic effort. The narrative framing is somewhat stylised, but the rules and questions are usable.
points: Leaders should ask what complexity a role is asking someone to hold now and what is about to arrive, then tailor support to each person's threshold state.
Different people need different interventions at the same moment: scaffolding for the overstretched, a forcing dilemma for the stuck, a wildcard project for the hesitant.
Anchoring practices are six standing questions about purpose, blockers, lived experience, cross-team effects, relationships and possible errors.
Reading the system means comparing espoused purpose and formal structure with what is actually lived and what actually gets things done.
Coherent, repeatable practice makes complex work livable in a way that heroic effort does not.
quotes: Maya realised: people don’t just grow into new levels. They pass through threshold states—stretch, tangle, drift, break, leap. Her job wasn’t to predict who would succeed. It was to notice who was ready to rehearse the next level.
Jo was burning out. Officially a Team Leader, but already forced to think like a Team of Teams leader. She didn’t need a break. She needed scaffolding.
Complex systems produce noise. Endless updates. Competing priorities. If you don’t anchor what matters, you drift.
These weren’t dashboards. They were anchors. Conversations to return to, again and again, until they became muscle memory.
By now, Maya knew the system didn’t behave like the org chart. It behaved like weather—shifting daily, sometimes hourly, with no respect for linear plans.
These weren’t tools. They were lenses. Ways of paying attention to what others ignored.
They didn’t make the work easier. But they made it livable—less about heroic effort, more about repeatable practice.
